title: What Remains Real When the World Changes
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Reflecting on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and on watching her own child grow up with no memory of that day, Schafer builds an explicit leadership argument out of two decades of accumulated disruption -- 9/11, wildfires, a pandemic, mass shootings. Her core claim is that institutional stability has repeatedly proven more fragile than assumed, but that ordinary individual action -- opening homes, showing up for neighbors, speaking for people being ignored -- has real, if partial, power even when it can't 'solve everything.' She crystallizes this into a definition she has used before: 'Leadership is love in action,' explicitly distinguishing this from softness -- it 'tells the truth with kindness,' 'draws a boundary with self-love,' and 'refuses to accept something that is causing harm.' The piece closes with three reflection questions aimed at leaders, asking what the uncertainty of recent years has revealed about what matters, where they've seen ordinary people create something better, and what ripple they want their own choices to send forward.
points: Schafer frames repeated institutional disruption (9/11, wildfire, pandemic, mass shootings) as evidence that assumed social stability is 'far more fragile than we imagined,' setting up her leadership argument.
Her central thesis, 'Leadership is love in action,' is explicitly defined against softness: it 'tells the truth with kindness,' sets boundaries, and refuses to accept ongoing harm.

She argues ordinary individual actions (opening one's home, showing up for a neighbor, speaking for an ignored voice) carry real leadership weight even though 'none of these actions solved everything.'
The piece closes with three structured reflection questions aimed at getting leaders to translate the essay's argument into personal practice.
quotes: So much of what many of us thought was secure, stable and enduring has proven to be far more fragile than we imagined.

They have shown me how much power exists in what ordinary people choose to do when something around them breaks. I have watched people open their homes. Show up for neighbors. Speak for someone whose voice is being ignored.

For years I have said: Leadership is love in action. The longer I live, the deeper my understand of what these words mean. Love in action is not about being soft. It tells the truth with kindness. It draws a boundary with self-love.
The world our children inherit will never be free of tragedy, disruption or uncertainty. We cannot promise them that. But we can influence what happens in response.
What kind of ripple do you want your choices to send forward now?
